UNIT 1 · LESSON 1
From idea to tested PCB

YOUR TASK
Explain the route from a circuit idea to a tested physical board.

Words you need
Schematic
A drawing of the parts and their electrical connections.
PCB layout
The physical placement of parts and copper connections on a printed circuit board.
Fabrication files
The layer and drill data sent to a manufacturer to make the bare board.
Assembly and test
Adding the parts, then checking that the real circuit behaves as intended.
How it works

This course uses a small battery-powered LED circuit as its running example. The schematic says what connects. Layout puts those connections on a board. Fabrication produces the board without components. Assembly and testing reveal how the real circuit behaves if you choose to build it.

Walk through an example

Suppose you have drawn a battery, switch, resistor, and LED in a schematic, but have no physical board design. The next job is to place those parts and route their copper connections in the PCB layout before you can make fabrication files.

LESSON 0.2
Work safely

YOUR TASK
State the supply you will use and one reason to stop before power.

Words you need
Power source
The part that supplies electrical energy. This course uses two AA cells in a removable external holder.
Short circuit
An unintended low-resistance path that can let too much current flow.
Continuity
A check for an electrical connection. Use the meter’s continuity setting only with power removed.
How it works

This course uses a small external holder with two alkaline AA cells. Keep cells out during wiring and continuity checks. A shorted battery can heat wiring or cells.

AA holder: empty
Cells out
Walk through an example

Suppose the assembled board needs an unpowered short check. Take both cells out of the holder before placing the meter probes on the supply contacts. An OFF switch alone does not remove power from every part of the board.

LESSON 0.3
Know your tools

YOUR TASK
List the tools and parts you have, and note anything missing.

Words you need
Jumper wire
A short removable wire used to connect points on a breadboard.
Breadboard
A reusable board with groups of holes joined inside, so you can test a circuit without soldering.
Meter probes
The two pointed leads of a multimeter; place them on the two points you want to compare.
Continuity mode
A meter setting that checks whether two points have a low-resistance connection. Use it with the cells removed.
How it works

A meter checks voltage and unpowered continuity. A breadboard tests temporary connections. KiCad creates the schematic and board files; a soldering iron assembles the physical board.

Meter
Breadboard
KiCad
Walk through an example

Suppose a jumper should join two breadboard rows. Remove the cells, set the meter to continuity, and touch one probe to each end of that intended path. A beep or low reading suggests a connection; no beep means you should inspect the wire and rows. DC voltage mode answers a different question: the voltage between two points while powered.

LESSON 1.1
Trace a closed loop

YOUR TASK
Trace a battery–switch–resistor–LED loop and mark where an open switch breaks it.

Words you need
Circuit loop
A complete conducting path from one battery terminal, through parts, and back to the other terminal.
Open switch
A switch position that breaks the conducting path.
How it works

A simple circuit needs a closed conducting path from one battery terminal, through the load, and back to the other. An open switch interrupts that path.

Resistor
Load
Battery
Walk through an example

Trace a path from battery positive through the switch, resistor, and LED to battery negative. If the switch opens, your finger can no longer trace a continuous route through the parts. The battery can still have voltage even though current through that loop stops.

coverage.title: Voltage and current
coverage.reading:
LESSON 1.2
Voltage and current

YOUR TASK
Describe two probe points for measuring voltage across a resistor.

Words you need
Current
The rate of electric charge flow through a branch, measured in amperes.
Voltage
The difference in electric potential between two points, measured in volts.
Across a part
One probe on each side of that part, so the meter compares its two ends.
How it works

Current describes charge flow through a branch. Voltage is a difference in electric potential between two points. A voltmeter therefore compares two probe locations.

V
Resistor
Voltage compares two points
Walk through an example

To learn the voltage across a resistor, place the two voltage probes on its two terminals. If you place them across the battery instead, you measure the supply voltage. Those are different measurements even in the same circuit.

LESSON 1.3
Units that matter

YOUR TASK
Convert 2.2 kΩ to ohms and 0.015 A to milliamperes, with units.

Words you need
Milli
One thousandth: 1 mA is 0.001 A.
Kilo
One thousand: 1 kΩ is 1000 Ω.
How it works

1 ampere equals 1000 milliamperes; 1 kilo-ohm equals 1000 ohms. Write the unit on every value so the scale of a calculation remains visible.

1 A
1000 mA
1 kΩ
1000 Ω
Walk through an example

Convert 5 mA to amperes before using Ohm’s law: 5 ÷ 1000 = 0.005 A. Convert 2.2 kΩ to ohms by multiplying by 1000: 2200 Ω. Keep units beside every number so a thousandfold mistake is visible.

coverage.title: Change a resistor
coverage.reading:
LESSON 1.4
Change a resistor

YOUR TASK
Predict the direction of current change before trying a different resistor in a model.

Words you need
Resistance
A measure of how strongly a resistor opposes current, in ohms (Ω).
Ohmic resistor
A resistor modeled by V = IR over the conditions used here. An LED does not behave like this resistor.
How it works

For an ideal fixed voltage across an ohmic resistor, I = V/R. Increasing R reduces I. The LED itself is not an ohmic resistor, so this is a model of the resistor portion.

I = V ÷ R
Use the voltage across the resistor
Walk through an example

If 2 V stays across a 100 Ω resistor, I = 2 ÷ 100 = 0.02 A. With 200 Ω at the same 2 V, I = 0.01 A. The larger resistance gives less current under the fixed-voltage assumption.

coverage.title: Use Ohm’s law
coverage.reading:
LESSON 1.5
Use Ohm’s law

YOUR TASK
Calculate the current through a 200 Ω resistor with 1 V across it.

Words you need
Ohm’s law
For a resistor, voltage V equals current I times resistance R: V = IR.
Rearrange
Solve the same relationship for the unknown: I = V/R or R = V/I.
How it works

Use I = V/R for an ohmic resistor and keep units visible. Rearrange to V = IR or R = V/I only after identifying what is known.

I = V ÷ R
Use the voltage across the resistor
Walk through an example

Suppose a 220 Ω resistor has 1.1 V across it. Divide 1.1 V by 220 Ω to get 0.005 A, or 5 mA. This calculates resistor current from the voltage actually across the resistor, not from battery voltage alone.

LESSON 1.6
Series, open, and short

YOUR TASK
Sketch a series loop, an open, and a bypass; explain what changes.

Words you need
Series path
Parts connected one after another so the same branch current goes through them.
Open
A break that prevents current in the path.
Bypass
An added route around a part. Around the resistor, it can remove the intended LED current limit.
How it works

A series path carries the same current through each component. An open breaks it. A low-resistance bypass across a load can create a dangerous short path.

Resistor
Load
Battery
Walk through an example

Imagine battery → switch → resistor → LED → battery. An open switch stops the loop. A wire across the resistor is different: the loop may remain closed while current avoids the resistor, which is unsafe for the LED.

LESSON 2.1
LED direction

YOUR TASK
Mark anode and cathode on a sketch of the planned LED and its schematic symbol.

Words you need
LED
A light-emitting diode; it has a direction and needs controlled current.
Anode and cathode
The LED’s two electrical terminals. Identify them from the exact part drawing and map them to the schematic and board.
How it works

An LED conducts primarily in one direction and needs a current-limiting element in this course circuit. Check both the schematic symbol and the exact part’s physical polarity marks.

Exact part + revision
Forward voltage: check test current
Maximum ratings: check conditions
Package: check dimensions + pins
Walk through an example

Before placing an LED, find its anode and cathode in the manufacturer drawing. Trace the intended current path on the schematic, then compare the board pad numbers and markings. If any of these disagree, pause and resolve the mismatch.

coverage.title: Read the datasheets
coverage.reading:
LESSON 2.2
Read the datasheets

YOUR TASK
Record the datasheet page and test conditions for one LED parameter and one battery parameter.

Words you need
Datasheet
The manufacturer’s document giving a part’s limits, measurements, and test conditions.
Typical
A representative value under stated conditions, not a guaranteed result for every part.
Nominal
A useful rated value, such as 1.5 V for an AA cell, not an exact voltage under every load.
How it works

A datasheet number is meaningful only with its conditions. The candidate Kingbright LED lists 1.9 V typical and 2.3 V maximum forward voltage at 10 mA and 25 °C; the AA cell’s 1.5 V is nominal.

Exact part + revision
Forward voltage: check test current
Maximum ratings: check conditions
Package: check dimensions + pins
Walk through an example

If a datasheet lists LED voltage at 10 mA and 25 °C, write those conditions next to the number. If your circuit runs at another current, treat that listed point as context and check the appropriate range before choosing a resistor.

Set a current target

State a tentative target and what evidence you still need before approving it.

Current target
The operating current you aim for when choosing the series resistor. It is a design choice.

Choose the resistor

YOUR TASK
Work the hypothetical calculation with units, then list what actual part data remains to be verified.

Words you need
Series resistor
A resistor in the LED’s current path that helps limit current.
Voltage across the resistor
Supply voltage minus the LED voltage in this simple series model.

LESSON 2.5
Check power and tolerance

YOUR TASK
Show the power calculation and cite the selected part’s rating, or mark the part unresolved.

Words you need
Power dissipation
Electrical energy converted to heat per second in a part, measured in watts.
Tolerance
The allowed variation around a part’s labeled value.
How it works

For a resistor, P = IV or I²R. Compare the computed worst-case dissipation with the exact resistor’s rating and tolerance in its datasheet.

Exact part + revision
Forward voltage: check test current
Maximum ratings: check conditions
Package: check dimensions + pins
Walk through an example

A 100 Ω resistor carrying 10 mA dissipates I²R = 0.010² × 100 = 0.010 W. Compare the worst plausible result with the exact resistor’s rating, allowing for the real supply and part values.

List the exact switch and holder part numbers or mark them unresolved.

Continuity test

With cells absent, verify expected connections and investigate possible supply shorts. A continuity beep means the meter found a low-resistance path, which may run through an installed part; it does not identify a solder bridge by itself. Confirm meter mode on a known connection.

Inspect
Assemble
Test
Walk through an example

Remove both cells and verify the meter’s continuity mode on a known connection. A beep between two pads means some low-resistance path exists, but an installed part or another route may be responsible. Trace the actual circuit before deciding a solder bridge is present.

LESSON 9.2
Recalculate

OPTIONAL HANDS-ON TASK
Record new calculations with units, assumptions, and a comparison to the old design.

Words you need
Recalculation
Repeating design math with the new part’s stated conditions and a range of supply values.
Assumption
A value used for a model that still needs verification against the exact part or hardware.
How it works

Recalculate the series resistor and power for the new LED using supply and LED ranges. State what is predicted and what still needs a real test.

New LED
Calculate
Update
Test
Walk through an example

For a hypothetical 3 V supply, 2 V LED drop, and 5 mA target, the resistor estimate is (3 − 2) ÷ 0.005 = 200 Ω. A new LED with a different assumed drop needs a fresh estimate and a range check, not a copied value.
